rewritten_text:
“So I own a few knights now,” I said as we rode away. “Who would have thought I'd live to include assets like that in my inventory? I won't know what to do with them, unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, sir, if you please, along with their squires.”

“A pretty good catch. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Oh, I did not understand you. I will tell you shortly.” Then, thoughtfully and quietly, she rolled the words delicately over her tongue. “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out. Yes, exactly: where do they hang out. It truly is a graceful, charming phrase, and very prettily expressed. I shall repeat it from time to time when I have nothing to do, and perhaps I will learn it. Where do they hang out. That's it! Already it rolls easily off my tongue, and since—”

“Don't forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes, the knights, you know. You were about to tell me about them. A while ago, remember? Figuratively speaking, the game's been called.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Step up to the plate. What I mean is, get started on the facts, and don't use up so much kindling lighting the fire. Tell me about the knights.”

“Gladly, and I will begin at once. So the two of them departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Good heavens!”

You see, I realized my mistake immediately. I'd started her machinery; I had only myself to blame. It would take her thirty days to reach those facts. Usually she began without an introduction and ended without a conclusion. Interrupt her, and she either continued without noticing, or answered in a word or two, then went back and repeated the entire sentence. Interruptions therefore only made things worse. Yet I had to interrupt, and frequently, to save my life: anyone would die with that monotony dripping onto them all day long.

“Good heavens!” I exclaimed in despair. She went straight back to the beginning.

“So the two of them departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. Then they reached an abbey of monks, where they were comfortably lodged. In the morning they attended mass in the abbey, and rode on until they entered a great forest. There Sir Gawaine noticed twelve lovely maidens in a valley beside a turret, with two armed knights on large horses; the maidens were walking back and forth by a tree.”

Well, I says I had needed that watermelon. But he said I hadn't needed it for escaping out of prison; that was the difference. If I'd wanted to put a knife inside it and sneak it in to Jim so he could kill the seneskal, he said, that would have been proper. So I left it there, though I couldn't see what good it done me to stand for a prisoner if every chance I got to grab a watermelon meant sitting down and chewing over such fine-spun distinctions.

Well, like I was saying, that morning we waited till everybody had got busy and there wasn't anybody to be seen in the yard; then Tom took the sack into the lean-to while I stayed a little ways off on the lookout. After a while he come back, and we sat on the woodpile for a talk. He says:

“We've got everything settled now but the tools, and that's easy enough.”

“Tools?” says I.

“Yes.”

“What tools do we need?”

“Why, digging tools. We ain't planning to gnaw him out, are we?”

“Ain't those old busted picks and such in there plenty good enough for digging a nigger out?” I says.

He turned toward me with such a pitying look it could have made a person cry, and says:

“Huck Finn, did you ever hear of any prisoner keeping picks and shovels and every modern convenience in his wardrobe for digging himself free? Now tell me, if there's any sense in you whatever, how would that give him a chance to be a hero? They might just as well hand him the key and have done. Picks and shovels! Why, they wouldn't let a king have those.”

“Well, then,” I says, “if picks and shovels ain't what we want, what is?”

“Two case-knives.”

“For digging away the foundations under that cabin?”

“Yes.”

“Hang it, Tom, that's foolishness.”

“It don't matter how foolish it sounds. It's the proper way, and the customary way. There ain't another way that I ever heard tell of, and I've read every book that tells about such things. They always dig their way out with a case-knife, and don't you think it's through dirt, either; mostly it's solid stone. It takes weeks upon weeks upon weeks, and forever besides. Just consider that prisoner down in the lowest dungeon of Castle Deef, in Marseilles harbor, who dug out like that. How long do you suppose he took?”

“I couldn't say.”

“Well, take a guess.”

“I don't know. Six weeks.”

In spite of everything, however, the boy became steadily paler, sadder, and more dispirited. She brought in hot baths, sitting baths, showers, and plunges. He continued as mournful as a hearse. She supplemented the water with a scant diet of oatmeal and blistering plasters. Estimating what he could hold as though he were a jug, she filled him daily with quack remedies for every ailment.

By now Tom had grown indifferent to persecution. This development struck alarm into the old lady's heart. Such indifference must be overcome, whatever the cost. At this point she first heard of Pain-killer, and immediately ordered a supply. Having tasted it, she overflowed with thankfulness. It was nothing less than liquid fire. She abandoned the water cure and all the other treatments, placing her whole confidence in Pain-killer. She administered a teaspoonful to Tom and waited in the greatest anxiety to see its effect. Instantly her worries ceased and peace returned to her soul: the “indifference” was shattered. Had she kindled a fire beneath the boy, he could not have displayed a more vigorous and frantic interest.

Tom decided that the time had come to rouse himself. For one in his blighted state, this existence might be romantic enough, but it was acquiring too little sentiment and far too much disturbing variety. He considered several means of escape, and finally conceived the idea of pretending to like Pain-killer. He begged for it so frequently that he grew troublesome, until his aunt told him to take it himself and stop pestering her. Had it been Sid, nothing would have troubled her satisfaction; since it was Tom, she kept a secret watch upon the bottle. The medicine certainly dwindled, she observed, but never imagined that he was using it to restore the health of a crack in the sitting-room floor.

One day, while Tom was administering a dose to the crack, his aunt's yellow cat approached, purring, greedily watching the teaspoon and pleading for a taste. Tom said:

“Don't beg for it, Peter, unless you really want some.”

Peter made it clear that he did.

“You'd better be certain.”

Peter was certain.

“Well, you asked, and I'll let you have it, for there's nothing stingy about me. Only, if it turns out you don't like it, don't go blaming anybody but yourself.”

Peter consented. Tom accordingly forced open his mouth and tipped in the Pain-killer. Peter leaped a couple of yards straight up, gave a war-whoop, and raced round and round the room, crashing into furniture, overturning flower-pots, and spreading destruction everywhere.
